n: These short and memorable songs were sung by pilgrims as they traveled to Jerusalem for the national festivals held three times each year ({{Deuteronomy 16:16|Deuteronomy 16:16}}). The title of these psalms includes a Hebrew word that can mean “steps” or “stairs.” Some scholars understand it to mean “going up to Jerusalem.” These psalms, often called the Songs of Ascents, lead the listener on a journey to Jerusalem to praise God for his goodness to Israel through history.

The mountains were known for idol worship ({{Deuteronomy 12:2|Deuteronomy 12:2}}), and Israel was drawn to the hilltop shrines ({{Hosea 4:13|Hosea 4:13}}). This verse can be seen as a rhetorical question expecting a "no" answer: The gods of the hilltop shrines cannot save anyone. 

Others understand the mountains to be a symbol of the Lord’s strength ({{Psalm 95:4|Psalm 95:4}}). In that case, the question would be taken literally (*From where does my help come?*), with the answer in the next verse.
The leader of the group of pilgrims uses word pictures to assure the group of the Lord’s presence during the journey.
God watches over his own, even and especially when they face many troubles ({{Psalm 12:5|Psalms 12:5}}, {{Psalm 12:7|7}}; {{Psalm 69:29|69:29}}; {{Psalm 91:14|91:14}}; {{Psalm 146:9|146:9}}).

- The Maker of heaven and earth ({{Psalm 121:2|Psalm 121:2}}) protects Israel. 

- God stands with Israel, offering support and care to the faithful (see {{Psalm 16:7-8|Psalm 16:7–8}}). 

- Both the sun and the moon were worshiped as gods in the ancient Near East. But God limits their power. They are part of creation and also praise the Lord ({{Psalm 148:3|Psalm 148:3}}).
The central sanctuary was *the house of the LORD*. This phrase first referred to the tabernacle ({{Exodus 23:19|Exodus 23:19}}; {{Exodus 34:26|34:26}}).

Jerusalem is presented here as the city of God, the city of David, and the center of faith. A group of pilgrims joyfully arrives in the city ({{Psalm 122:1-2|Psalm 122:1–2}}). The psalmist praises Jerusalem ({{Psalm 122:3-5|Psalm 122:3–5}}) and prays for the city’s peace ({{Psalm 122:6-9|122:6–9}}).
Several psalms celebrate or look forward to being inside the gates of the city ({{Psalm 9:14|Psalms 9:14}}; {{Psalm 87:2|87:2}}; {{Psalm 100:4|100:4}}; {{Psalm 118:19|118:19}}).
In the time of David and Solomon, people knew Jerusalem as a safe place ({{1 Kings 10:6-7|1 Kings 10:6–7}}).
Jerusalem can represent God’s heavenly dwelling place. David became the model for the rulers God chooses.

- Each person in Israel belonged to a tribe, and all tribes belonged to the Lord. 

- Giving thanks means presenting an offering acceptable to the Lord ({{Psalm 50:14|Psalms 50:14}}, {{Psalm 50:23|23}}; {{Psalm 100:4|100:4}}; {{Psalm 118:19|118:19}}). 

- *as a testimony for Israel*: See {{Exodus 23:17|Exodus 23:17}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:16|Deuteronomy 16:16}}.
*the thrones of judgment stand*: In the time of David and Solomon ({{1 Kings 3:28|1 Kings 3:28}}), Jerusalem was known for wisdom and justice. It will be like that again ({{Isaiah 9:7|Isaiah 9:7}}).
Prayers for the peace of Jerusalem are motivated by love of family and God’s sanctuary.

This lament about the psalmist's humble position shows strong trust in the Lord ({{Psalm 123:1-2|Psalm 123:1–2}}). The psalmist prays for God's favor on the community because evil surrounds them ({{Psalm 123:3-4|Psalm 123:3–4}}). The poet looks beyond Jerusalem ({{Psalm 122:1-9|Psalm 122}}) to God's throne in heaven.
The negative rhetorical questions emphasize the positive idea that the Lord was indeed on their side.
This thanksgiving song describes what might happen if the Lord were not present with his people.
*the raging waters*: The enemies could have defeated the Israelites and destroyed them if the Lord had not supported his people (compare {{Psalm 69:15|Psalm 69:15}}; {{Jeremiah 46:8|Jeremiah 46:8}}).

The enemies of God's people were like lions or bears that tear prey with their teeth (see {{Psalm 57:4|Psalm 57:4}}; {{Proverbs 28:15|Proverbs 28:15}}). The Lord shut their mouths ({{Daniel 6:22|Daniel 6:22}}).
The psalmist expresses the community's trust in the Lord's protection ({{Psalm 125:1-2|Psalm 125:1–2}}) and prays for peace ({{Psalm 125:3-5|125:3–5}}).
*surrounds*: God guards and protects like a wall of fire ({{Zechariah 2:5|Zechariah 2:5}}).
The godly may be tempted to abandon God’s ways because of pressure from others or from the surrounding culture.
People who do not follow the "straight paths" are foolish ({{Proverbs 2:12-15|Proverbs 2:12–15}}). God gives his goodness to the godly (see {{Psalm 122:6-9|Psalm 122:6–9}}).

The Lord brought about Israel’s restoration from exile, just as he had brought Israel out of Egypt ({{Psalm 114:1|Psalm 114:1}}). The restoration transformed the weeping of the Lord’s people into laughter and showed the Lord’s character to the nations ({{Psalm 9:11|Psalm 9:11}}; {{Psalm 64:9|64:9}}; {{Isaiah 12:4|Isaiah 12:4}}).
This psalm celebrates Israel's return from exile ({{Psalm 126:1-3|Psalm 126:1–3}}). The psalmist then prays that God will fully restore the people ({{Psalm 126:4-6|Psalm 126:4–6}}).

- The prophets had spoken of the restoration as a time when the wilderness would change into the garden of Eden ({{Isaiah 51:3|Isaiah 51:3}}; {{Ezekiel 47:1-23|Ezekiel 47}}). However, the reality was far from paradise. Here, the restoration community prays for complete redemption (see {{Haggai 2:19|Haggai 2:19}}). 

- *like streams in the Negev*: Seasonal rains filled the dry riverbeds (*wadis*), making the land green again. The prayer seeks a similar change in Israel’s fortunes, fulfilling the imagery of the "Second Exodus" in Isaiah (see "The Promise of a Second Exodus" Theme Note). 

- *carrying sheaves of grain*: This harvest represents God's complete restoration.

- *Unless*: These conditional statements emphasize that the Lord is the one who protects the city (compare {{Psalm 124:1-2|Psalm 124:1–2}}). 

- Human effort achieves nothing unless the Lord blesses it (see {{Psalm 44:3|Psalm 44:3}}). 

- *you rise early and stay up late*: This phrase describes people who work constantly and live with pressure and competition.

- Those whom God loves can rest and sleep in peace ({{Psalm 3:5|Psalm 3:5}}; {{Psalm 4:8|4:8}}).

Blessings and protection come from God. Without his presence, success is not possible ({{Psalm 127:1-2|Psalm 127:1–2}}). This is especially true for children, who are gifts from God ({{Psalm 127:3-5|Psalm 127:3–5}}).

Children are one of God’s blessings. In Hebrew, the word for children (*banim*) sounds like the word for builders (*bonim*; {{Psalm 127:1|Psalm 127:1}}). This wordplay shows that having children helps build a family.

*Like arrows*: The image compares children to arrows in a warrior’s hand. Children strengthen and support the family and help defend its honor when others accuse or oppose them (compare {{Psalm 120:4|Psalms 120:4}}; {{Psalm 7:12-13|7:12–13}}).
*eating the fruit of your labor*: This means gaining benefit from whatever work one does.

The godly, who fear the Lord, will know true happiness ({{Psalm 128:1-2|Psalm 128:1–2}}). The Lord is with them (see {{Psalm 127:1-2|Psalm 127:1–2}}), strengthens their family life ({{Psalm 128:3-4|128:3–4}}), and blesses them for generations ({{Psalm 128:5-6|128:5–6}}).

Children are like strong young olive trees because they are full of potential. Olive oil symbolizes God's blessing ({{Psalm 104:15|Psalm 104:15}}; {{Numbers 18:12|Numbers 18:12}}; {{Jeremiah 31:12|Jeremiah 31:12}}; {{Haggai 2:19|Haggai 2:19}}).

- God will continually bless those who fear him ({{Psalm 133:3|Psalm 133:3}}) from his dwelling in Zion ({{Psalm 20:2|20:2}}; {{Psalm 50:2|50:2}}; {{Psalm 110:2|110:2}}), no matter where they live. 

- *children's children*: God's blessings continue through generations for those who are faithful ({{Psalm 79:12-13|Psalms 79:12–13}}; {{Psalm 89:1|89:1}}; {{Psalm 100:4-5|100:4–5}}; {{Psalm 103:17-19|103:17–19}}).
Israel’s earliest years as a nation took place while the people were living in Egypt.

The psalmist briefly reviews Israel’s history of trouble ({{Psalm 129:1-2|Psalm 129:1–2}}) and redemption ({{Psalm 129:3-4|129:3–4}}). He ends with curses against the enemies and blessings on the godly ({{Psalm 129:5-6|Psalm 129:5–6}}).
*The LORD is righteous*: He rescued Israel from Egypt, from many enemy attacks, and from the Babylonian exile.
Grass on a rooftop had shallow roots and would scorch easily. A crop was ignored by the harvester when the yield was low. The enemies who had sown hurt among God’s people would gain little.

A cry from the depths comes from a place of deep distress (compare {{Psalm 69:2|Psalm 69:2}}, {{Psalm 69:14|14}}; {{Isaiah 51:10|Isaiah 51:10}}; {{Ezekiel 27:34|Ezekiel 27:34}}). Feeling weak, the psalmist prays for God's favor.

Beginning with himself as a representative of the community, the psalmist cries for God’s mercy ({{Psalm 130:1-3|Psalm 130:1–3}}) out of deep distress. He places his hope in the Lord ({{Psalm 130:4-6|Psalm 130:4–6}}), trusting that the Lord will rescue in his own time and way. With this confidence, the psalmist invites Israel to wait for the Lord ({{Psalm 130:7-8|Psalm 130:7–8}}).
The psalmist knows that his sins make him guilty and deserving of God’s judgment.
The good news comes in God’s readiness to forgive sinners. His grace encourages people to fear him and hope in him.

Israel is encouraged to hope in the Lord ({{Psalm 9:18|Psalms 9:18}}; {{Psalm 27:14|27:14}}; {{Psalm 131:3|131:3}}) because the Lord pays the high price for redemption and removes the sin that separates humans from him (see also {{Psalm 111:9|Psalm 111:9}}; {{Exodus 6:6-8|Exodus 6:6–8}}; {{2 Samuel 7:23-24|2 Samuel 7:23–24}}; {{Isaiah 43:1-4|Isaiah 43:1–4}}; {{Titus 2:14|Titus 2:14}}; {{Hebrews 9:12|Hebrews 9:12}}; {{1 Peter 1:18|1 Peter 1:18}}).
